name: McKinsey & Company
seo_title: McKinsey interview process: what to expect
description: What McKinsey & Company's own careers pages say about applying: the Solve game, problem-solving and experience interviews, and its rules on AI.
intro: This guide sums up what McKinsey & Company's own careers pages say about applying for a consulting role, from the Solve assessment to the problem-solving and personal experience interviews. It reflects those pages as we checked them on 15 October 2026. McKinsey says its process and timeline differ by role and location, so check its careers site for your office and role before you apply.

items.text: McKinsey's careers FAQs say the recruitment process and timeline differ by role and location, and that if you are invited to interview, your recruiter will tell you what to expect and roughly when each step happens.

For consulting roles, McKinsey says it may ask you to take a test or play a game as part of your application, depending on the role, and that these assessments focus on job-related skills such as problem solving.

The FAQs say people who finished an undergraduate degree within the past four years are typically considered for business analyst roles (called fellows in some offices), while people with a bachelor's degree and at least four years of work experience, or an advanced degree such as an MBA, JD, MD or PhD, typically join as associates.

There is one application portal for generalist and practice roles. You can list up to three office or practice preferences and share 60 points between them to show how strongly you prefer each, and in the end you are invited to interview for one location or practice.
McKinsey says every office looks for the same qualities in a CV and a candidate, although some locations require the local language.
McKinsey describes Solve as a gamified assessment of problem-solving ability and says it is a step in the process for most consulting roles.
McKinsey says there is no need to prepare for Solve, and that your Solve result is considered together with the rest of your application and any other assessments you are asked to take.
McKinsey's Solve FAQs say you need no business knowledge or gaming experience, and that each task starts with an untimed tutorial explaining what to do.
The length of the assessment is given in your invitation email.
Solve can be taken only on a PC or Mac, not on an iPad or phone. A tech check runs before you start, sound is not needed and a mouse is optional.
Solve can be taken in English, Spanish, Portuguese or Japanese.
The FAQs say scenarios vary so that no two candidates get the same combination of data, and that you may be asked at random to do an extra task in person or to explain the logic you used.
If something goes wrong technically, the FAQs say to contact McKinsey's Solve support team at the time it happens, because a reset cannot be allowed afterwards if you did not.
For technical roles, McKinsey says you may instead be invited to a hands-on technical assessment, for example in programming, data analysis or system design.

For most client-facing roles, McKinsey says you will have personal experience interviews and problem-solving interviews, and for some roles an expertise interview as well. Your recruiter confirms the details in advance.

McKinsey says the problem-solving interview, sometimes called a case interview, is a discussion of a typical McKinsey client scenario, in which you are given a business case so the interviewer can see how you approach complex problems.
McKinsey says there is not one logical solution, and asks candidates to listen carefully and give answers tailored to the case rather than standard frameworks.
McKinsey says the expertise interview, used for some roles, explores how your experience and skills will help you do well in the role.
McKinsey says the personal experience interview (PEI) is about your experiences, both achievements and challenges, and that you should be ready to discuss them in detail, focusing on your own role.
It suggests choosing experiences that genuinely mattered to you and leading with your reasoning, not just your actions, and says to expect a conversation rather than to present a rehearsed story.
McKinsey suggests coming with two personal examples for each of the four areas its PEI covers, with the details of the challenge and the specific actions you took.

McKinsey says you may hear about its values during your interviews, such as its culture of apprenticeship and the expectation to engage and dissent, and encourages you to discuss them with your interviewers.

sections.heading: Rules on AI, calculators and notes

items.text: McKinsey says using AI to polish your CV, practise interview questions or explain concepts and frameworks while you prepare is encouraged.
It does not allow using AI to exaggerate or invent achievements, to generate answers in real time during an interview, or during assessments unless this is specifically permitted.

McKinsey's assessment integrity page says that in any assessment or interview, including virtual ones, you take part alone, use one screen, stay on camera without a virtual background or blurring, and use only pen and paper for notes and calculations.

The same page says calculators, apps, websites, generative AI and prepared notes are not allowed, that McKinsey may ask to look at your notes to understand your thinking, and that you should discard your notes afterwards.
It also asks candidates not to record any part of an assessment or interview, take screenshots, or share its content, such as specific questions or problem-solving scenarios, with others.
Unless McKinsey has approved an accommodation for a disability, it says breaking these rules may lead to disqualification, a withdrawn offer, limits on future applications or legal action.
If you need an accommodation because of a disability, health condition or specific learning difficulty, McKinsey's Solve FAQs say to speak to your recruiter.
McKinsey's interviewing page has five practice cases with suggested answers, called Beautify, Diconsa, Electro-Light, Transforming a national education system and Talbot Trucks.
McKinsey says working through them will help you get used to the kind of questions it asks in the problem-solving interview.

Its general advice for interviews is to relax and be yourself, bring questions for your interviewers, and come ready to talk about your experiences, skills and achievements. It says your recruiter will also guide you.
For virtual interviews, McKinsey suggests a quiet, private space, keeping a pen, paper, water and your laptop charger close by, keeping your camera on and doing a test run of your video first.

It also asks you to switch off any AI software already installed, such as note-taking tools or virtual assistants, because it may record or assist with the interview, and to ask the interviewer to repeat a question if it is not clear.

practice_advice: Practise saying your structure out loud before you start any analysis, so the interviewer can follow your plan.
Do short, timed mental maths drills most days, with pen and paper only. Mock Partner's drills cover mental maths, chart reading and market sizing.
Run full practice cases from the opening question to a final recommendation, and finish each one with a summary of a minute or less.
Pick a few experiences from your own life that really mattered to you, and practise talking through what you did and why, so you can answer follow-up questions instead of reciting a script.
After every practice case, write down one thing to improve and focus on it in the next one.
